criteria.text: The response says that Varga's acquisition of Halvorsen's stock is a Change of Control that needs Crestline's prior written consent under Section 15.4 of the Distribution Agreement. It also says that Section 3.5 of the Seller Disclosure Schedule wrongly describes the Crestline agreement as notice-only or no consent required. It explains that this exposes Halvorsen to termination or a termination fee and/or an inaccurate consents representation to Varga.

The response says that Section 14.2 of the Distribution Agreement, read with the Section 1.1 definition of 'Qualified Transferee', lets Crestline assign the agreement without Halvorsen's consent to any distributor of laboratory or diagnostic products in the Territory. It explains that this could include a Halvorsen competitor or a competitor's affiliate, because the definition does not exclude competitors.

The response says that Section 3 of the First Amendment restates Section 12.3 so that only breaches of Section 9 (confidentiality) are excluded from the liability cap. It says this drops the carve-outs for intellectual property (Section 10) and indemnification (Section 11). It explains that the amendment controls under the order-of-precedence clause in Section 17.5, so those claims against Crestline are now capped.
The response states that the original Section 12.3 of the Distribution Agreement excluded from the cap the breaches of Sections 9 and 10 and the indemnification obligations under Section 11.
The response states that the liability cap in Section 12.2 equals the amounts paid or payable to the Supplier in the 12 months preceding the claim.
The response is organised as a memo that lists the issues separately. For each issue it gives the document and section, why it matters for Halvorsen, and a recommended fix.
The response does not conclude that the Varga acquisition requires only notice to Crestline, or that no Crestline consent is needed.
The response does not conclude that the original Section 12.3 carve-outs for intellectual property and indemnity still apply despite the First Amendment.
